once.soru: Paper releases heat when it burns, but it doesn't catch fire by itself on a desk. Why?

secenekler.neden: Exothermic reactions also have an activation energy. A match supplies this energy.
Burning releases heat, so it is exothermic.
There is enough oxygen in the air.

cards.p: The forward and reverse reactions pass over the same hill. The difference gives the heat of reaction: ΔH = Ea,forward − Ea,reverse. In an exothermic reaction, Ea,forward is smaller.

once.soru: In an exothermic reaction, from which direction is it harder to climb the hill?

secenekler.neden: The products have lower energy. Climbing the hill from the products takes more energy.
The reactants are at high energy and closer to the top.
The reactants and products have different energies, so the heights differ.

cards.p: The rate law has the form rate = k[A]x[B]y. x and y are found by experiment, and in elementary reactions they equal the coefficients. Solids and pure liquids are not written in the rate law.

cards.key: The overall order is x + y. k doesn't change with concentration, but it does change with temperature and catalysts.

once.soru: In the one-step reaction 2A → B, if [A] doubles, by what factor does the rate change?

secenekler.neden: In an elementary reaction the order equals the coefficient, so rate = k[A]². The rate goes up 2² = 4 times.
The rate is proportional to the square of [A], not linear.
When concentration rises, the number of collisions rises.

etk.soru: For this reaction rate = k[X][Y]<sup>2</sup>, k = 2 L²/(mol²·s). Double [X] or [Y]: by what factor does the rate go up?

cards.key: If the concentration goes up n times, the rate goes up nˣ times. If doubling the concentration makes the rate 4 times larger, x = 2.

cards.p: The unit of rate is always M/s. The unit of k depends on the overall order. It is M/s for zero order, 1/s for first order and 1/(M·s) for second order.

cards.key: If the unit of k is M/s, the reaction is zero order. Then the rate doesn't depend on concentration.

once.soru: For rate = k[A], rate is in M/s and [A] in M. What is the unit of k?

secenekler.neden: k = rate / [A] = (M/s) / M = 1/s.
M/s is the unit of rate. The unit of k comes from dividing it by [A].
k relates to rate, so its unit must include time.

cards.p: Most reactions happen in several steps, and these steps are called the mechanism. The overall rate is set by the slowest step, the one with the largest Ea. The rate law is written from the reactants of this step.

once.soru: On a production line, three machines work in sequence: 100, 10 and 50 items per hour. Which one sets the speed of the line?

secenekler.neden: Items pile up at the slowest machine. The line can't run faster than this machine.
The fast machine waits for the slow one after it.
In sequential work, the slowest step sets the overall speed.

cards.p: Reactions between oppositely charged ions are very fast. The more bonds that must break, the slower the reaction. When concentration rises, the number of collisions rises and so does the rate.

once.soru: Charcoal burns slowly in air but quickly with a bright flame in pure oxygen. Why?

secenekler.neden: There is more O₂ per unit volume. So the number of collisions and the rate go up.
Ea is changed by a catalyst, not by concentration.

secenekler.yazi: The charcoal gives off more heat
secenekler.neden: It is the same reaction, and the heat released is the same. Only the rate is different.

cards.p: When temperature rises, particles speed up. The main effect, though, is that a larger fraction of particles exceeds E<sub>a</sub>. E<sub>a</sub> doesn't change, but k gets larger. That's why the rate goes up in both exothermic and endothermic reactions.
cards.key: Roughly, every 10 °C rise about doubles the rate of many reactions.

cards.p: Heterogeneous reactions, such as solid–solution ones, happen only at the contact surface. Grinding a solid into powder increases the surface, so collisions and the rate go up.

once.soru: What do preservatives added to food do to spoilage reactions?

secenekler.neden: Preservatives are inhibitors and delay spoilage.
A substance that speeds up a reaction is a catalyst.
If they had no effect, they wouldn't be added to food.

cards.p:
• Rate is the change in concentration per unit time, and the rates of substances are proportional to the coefficients.
• An effective collision needs enough energy and the right orientation.
• ΔH = Ea,forward − Ea,reverse. A catalyst lowers Ea and doesn't change ΔH.
• The rate law is rate = k[A]x[B]y, and the orders are found by experiment.

quiz.q: The rate law of X + 2Y → Z is rate = k[X]<sup>2</sup>[Y]. At the same temperature, if [X] is tripled and [Y] is halved, by what factor does the rate change?
quiz.e: The rate changes by 3² × ½ = 4.5 times. The orders come from the rate law, not from the coefficients of the equation.

quiz.q: For a reaction between a solid and a solution, sort each change by its effect on the rate.
quiz.e: As temperature rises, more particles exceed E<sub>a</sub>. A catalyst opens a path with lower E<sub>a</sub>. A powdered solid has a larger contact surface. An inhibitor, low temperature and small contact surface slow the reaction.

quiz.q: For a reaction, E<sub>a,forward</sub> = 120 kJ and E<sub>a,reverse</sub> = 45 kJ. What is ΔH for the reaction in kJ?
quiz.e: ΔH = E<sub>a,forward</sub> − E<sub>a,reverse</sub> = 120 − 45 = +75 kJ. The result is positive, so the reaction is endothermic. The products are 75 kJ higher than the reactants.

quiz.q: The reaction 2NO + Br<sub>2</sub> → 2NOBr has two steps: 1) NO + Br<sub>2</sub> → NOBr<sub>2</sub> (slow), 2) NOBr<sub>2</sub> + NO → 2NOBr (fast). Which is the rate law?
quiz.e: The slow step sets the rate. The reactants of this step are one NO and one Br<sub>2</sub>, so rate = k[NO][Br<sub>2</sub>]. The second NO enters in the fast step and doesn't affect the rate.
y: You took the exponents from the coefficients of the net equation. The rate law is written from the slow step, which has only one NO.
NOBr<sub>2</sub> is an intermediate. Intermediates are not written in the rate law.
Br<sub>2</sub> takes part in the slow step and can't be left out of the rate law.

kimyasal-denge.title: Chemical equilibrium
kimyasal-denge.summary: Dynamic equilibrium, K and Q, Le Chatelier's principle and the solubility product.

cards.p: In a closed container many reactions run in both directions (⇌). When the forward and reverse rates become equal, equilibrium is reached. At this point the concentrations no longer change, but they don't have to be equal.

cards.p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD we write Kc = [C]c[D]d / [A]a[B]b. Products go in the numerator and reactants in the denominator. Solids and pure liquids are left out.

cards.key: As long as the temperature doesn't change, Kc stays constant. Gases and (aq) species go into the expression, but substances in (s) and (l) states don't.

once.soru: For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), which substance appears in the Kc expression?

secenekler.neden: The concentration of a solid is constant and isn't written in the expression. So Kc = [CO₂].
CaCO₃ and CaO are solids, so they don't go into the K expression.
Solids are left out, and gases are written.

cards.h: The relationship between Kp and Kc
cards.p: For gas reactions, K can also be written with partial pressures, and this is called Kp. Kp = Kc·(RT)Δn. Here Δn is the moles of gaseous products minus the moles of gaseous reactants.

once.soru: In H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, the moles of gas are equal on both sides. How are Kp and Kc related?

secenekler.neden: Δn = 2 − 2 = 0. Since (RT)⁰ = 1, Kp = Kc.
That can happen when Δn > 0.
That can happen when Δn < 0.

cards.h: What does the size of K tell us?
cards.p: If K is very large, products dominate at equilibrium and the reaction almost goes to completion. If K is very small, reactants remain the majority. K says nothing about the rate of the reaction.

once.soru: A reaction has K = 10¹⁰. What can be said about this reaction?

secenekler.neden: A large K shows that the numerator, the products, dominate.
K says nothing about rate. Reaching equilibrium could take years.
That happens when K is very small.

cards.p: If the equation is reversed, the new constant is 1/K. If the coefficients are multiplied by n, it becomes Kn. If two equations are added, the constants are multiplied to give K1·K2.

cards.key: If the coefficients are halved, it becomes √K. When equations are added, the Ks are multiplied, not added.

once.soru: For A ⇌ B, K = 4. What is K for B ⇌ A?

secenekler.neden: In the reverse reaction the numerator and denominator swap. So K' = 1/K.
When the equation is reversed, the expression is inverted too.
K is a ratio of concentrations and can't be negative.

cards.p: Writing the current concentrations into the K expression gives Q. If Q < K, the reaction runs forward, and if Q > K, it runs in reverse. If Q = K, the system is at equilibrium.

etk.soru: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, K<sub>c</sub> = 64 at this temperature. Change the current concentrations: Q = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) tells the direction of the reaction.
yorum: Q < K: the reaction runs forward.
Q = K: the system is at equilibrium.
Q > K: the reaction runs in reverse.

cards.key: A reaction always moves in the direction that brings Q closer to K.

cards.p: According to Le Chatelier's principle, if a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that reduces the disturbance. If a substance is added, it shifts toward the side that uses it up. If a substance is removed, it shifts toward the side that produces it.

cards.key: If the temperature is constant, K doesn't change. Adding a solid or a pure liquid doesn't shift the equilibrium.

once.soru: You add some more of a reactant to a container at equilibrium. Which way does the equilibrium shift?

secenekler.neden: The equilibrium shifts toward the side that uses up the added substance, which is forward.
The reverse direction produces reactants. That would increase the excess substance even more.
Adding a gaseous or dissolved reactant does shift the equilibrium.

cards.p: At constant temperature, when the volume shrinks the pressure rises, and the equilibrium shifts toward the side with fewer moles of gas. If the moles are equal, there is no shift. Adding an inert gas at constant volume doesn't shift the equilibrium either.

etk.soru: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ. For each change, which way does the equilibrium shift?
ogeler: The pressure rises. The equilibrium shifts toward the side with fewer moles of gas (2 mol NH₃).
The reaction is exothermic. When the temperature rises, the equilibrium shifts toward the heat-absorbing direction, which is reverse.
The pressure falls. The equilibrium shifts toward the side with more moles of gas (4 mol).
A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor.
The partial pressures don't change, so the equilibrium doesn't shift.

cards.key: If an inert gas is added at constant pressure, the volume grows. Then the equilibrium shifts toward the side with more moles.

cards.p: Only temperature changes K. Heating shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction. So for an exothermic reaction K decreases, and for an endothermic one it increases. A catalyst doesn't shift the equilibrium.

cards.key: For an exothermic reaction, heating speeds it up but makes K smaller.

cards.p: Ammonia is made from N₂ and H₂. The reaction is exothermic and the moles of gas decrease. So high pressure raises the yield. A temperature of about 450 °C and an iron catalyst are a compromise between rate and yield.

cards.p: A slightly soluble salt is in equilibrium with its ions in a saturated solution. For AgCl we write Ksp = [Ag+][Cl−]. If the solubility is s, Ksp = s² for AB type salts and 4s³ for AB₂ type.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='24' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)</text><text x='160' y='46' font-size='14' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>K<tspan font-size='10' baseline-shift='sub'>sp</tspan> = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻]</text><rect x='10' y='58' width='145' height='98' rx='6' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='var(--c1)'/><text x='82' y='78' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>AB type (AgCl)</text><text x='82' y='99' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>[A⁺] = s,  [B⁻] = s</text><text x='82' y='123' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>K<tspan font-size='10' baseline-shift='sub'>sp</tspan> = s²</text><text x='82' y='143' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>s = √K<tspan font-size='10' baseline-shift='sub'>sp</tspan></text><rect x='165' y='58' width='145' height='98' rx='6' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='var(--c5)'/><text x='237' y='78' font-size='12' fill='var(--c5)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>AB₂ type (CaF₂)</text><text x='237' y='99' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>[Ca²⁺] = s,  [F⁻] = 2s</text><text x='237' y='123' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>K<tspan font-size='10' baseline-shift='sub'>sp</tspan> = s·(2s)² = 4s³</text><text x='237' y='143' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>s = ∛(K<tspan font-size='10' baseline-shift='sub'>sp</tspan> / 4)</text><text x='160' y='175' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>AgCl at 25 °C: K<tspan font-size='10' baseline-shift='sub'>sp</tspan> = 1.8×10⁻¹⁰</text><text x='160' y='196' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>s ≈ 1.3×10⁻⁵ mol/L</text></svg>
cards.key: Ksp is short for solubility product. You can compare Ksp and solubility directly only for salts of the same type.

once.soru: In the equilibrium AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻, why isn't AgCl written in the Ksp expression?

secenekler.neden: The concentration of a solid is constant and isn't written in the K expression.
It's left out because it is a solid, not because it dissolves slightly.
Dissolved ions are written. What is left out is the solid form of the substance.

cards.p: If the ion product in a mixture is Q > Ksp, a precipitate forms. If one of the salt's ions is already in the solution (a common ion), the salt dissolves less.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><circle cx='18' cy='22' r='5' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.85'/><text x='30' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>Q < K<tspan font-size='10' baseline-shift='sub'>sp</tspan></text><text x='110' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>unsaturated: no precipitate</text><circle cx='18' cy='44' r='5' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.85'/><text x='30' y='48' font-size='12' fill='var(--c5)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>Q = K<tspan font-size='10' baseline-shift='sub'>sp</tspan></text><text x='110' y='48' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>saturated: equilibrium</text><circle cx='18' cy='66' r='5' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.85'/><text x='30' y='70' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>Q > K<tspan font-size='10' baseline-shift='sub'>sp</tspan></text><text x='110' y='70' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>precipitate forms</text><line x1='10' y1='92' x2='310' y2='92' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='160' y='112' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Common ion effect: solubility of AgCl (25 °C)</text><text x='14' y='138' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>pure water</text><rect x='86' y='126' width='160' height='16' rx='3' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.55'/><text x='252' y='138' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>1.3×10⁻⁵ M</text><text x='14' y='166' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>0.1 M NaCl</text><rect x='86' y='154' width='4' height='16' rx='1' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.8'/><text x='96' y='166' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>1.8×10⁻⁹ M  (about 7000 times less)</text><text x='160' y='192' font-size='11' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Extra Cl⁻ pushes the equilibrium left, so AgCl dissolves less.</text></svg>
cards.key: If Q = Ksp, the solution is saturated. When solutions are mixed, the volume grows. So calculate Q with the diluted concentrations.

once.soru: Can you dissolve more AgCl in pure water or in NaCl solution?

secenekler.neden: The Cl⁻ in NaCl pushes the equilibrium left. So AgCl dissolves less in that solution.
The common Cl⁻ ion lowers solubility, it doesn't raise it.
A common ion lowers solubility.

cards.p:
• At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations are constant.
• Solids and pure liquids are not written in the K expression.
• If Q < K the reaction runs forward, and if Q > K it runs in reverse.
• Equilibrium shifts in the direction that reduces the disturbance, and only temperature changes K.
• If Q > Ksp, a precipitate forms. A common ion lowers solubility.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='20' font-size='14' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Chemical equilibrium</text><rect x='10' y='30' width='146' height='70' rx='8' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.1' stroke='var(--c1)'/><text x='83' y='60' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Forward rate = reverse rate</text><text x='83' y='80' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>concentrations constant</text><rect x='164' y='30' width='146' height='70' rx='8' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.1' stroke='var(--c3)'/><text x='237' y='60' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Q < K → forward</text><text x='237' y='80' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Q > K → reverse</text><rect x='10' y='112' width='146' height='70' rx='8' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.1' stroke='var(--c2)'/><text x='83' y='142' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Toward reducing the disturbance</text><text x='83' y='162' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Only T changes K</text><rect x='164' y='112' width='146' height='70' rx='8' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.1' stroke='var(--c5)'/><text x='237' y='142' font-size='12' fill='var(--c5)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Q > K<tspan font-size='10' baseline-shift='sub'>sp</tspan> → precipitate</text><text x='237' y='162' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>common ion lowers s</text><text x='160' y='196' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Solids and pure liquids are not written in the K expression.</text></svg>

quiz.q: At constant temperature, 1 mol of N₂O₄ is placed in a closed 2 L container: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). At equilibrium the container holds 0.4 mol of NO₂. What is K<sub>c</sub>?
quiz.e: When 0.4 mol of NO₂ forms, 0.2 mol of N₂O₄ is used up and 0.8 mol of N₂O₄ remains. [N₂O₄] = 0.4 M and [NO₂] = 0.2 M, so K<sub>c</sub> = 0.2² / 0.4 = 0.1.

quiz.q: The reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is exothermic. Sort each change by where it shifts the equilibrium.
quiz.e: Added N₂ is used up, and removed NH₃ is produced again. When the volume shrinks, the equilibrium shifts toward the side with fewer moles (2 mol gas). Heating shifts an exothermic equilibrium toward the reactants. A catalyst and He added at constant volume don't shift the equilibrium.

quiz.q: In a saturated solution of a slightly soluble AB<sub>2</sub> salt, the molar solubility is s = 1×10<sup>−3</sup> M. What is K<sub>sp</sub>?
quiz.e: [A<sup>2+</sup>] = s and [B<sup>−</sup>] = 2s. So K<sub>sp</sub> = s·(2s)<sup>2</sup> = 4s<sup>3</sup> = 4×10<sup>−9</sup>.
y: You used s² as for the AB type. AB<sub>2</sub> has two anions, so the result is 4s³.
You forgot to square 2s. The right answer is s·(2s)² = 4s³.
You used just s³. [B<sup>−</sup>] = 2s, so its square is 4s², and the result is 4s³.

quiz.q: For A(g) + B(g) ⇌ 2C(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 4 at a certain temperature. At one moment a 1 L container holds 1 mol of A, 1 mol of B and 4 mol of C. Which is true?
o: It runs in reverse, C decreases
quiz.e: Q = 4² / (1·1) = 16. Since Q > K, the reaction runs in reverse. C is used up until Q drops to 4.
y: Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 4²/(1·1) = 16. Since Q ≠ K, the system is not at equilibrium.
Q = 16, which is larger than K = 4. There is too much product, so the reaction runs in reverse.
When calculating Q, [C] must be squared. So the result is 4² = 16, not 4.

asit-baz.title: Acids, bases and salts
asit-baz.summary: Learn the definitions of acids and bases, pH, Ka, neutralization, salts and titration.

cards.p: Acids taste sour. Solutions of bases taste bitter and feel slippery. Dyes that change color in acids and bases are called indicators. Litmus turns red in acid and blue in base.

cards.key: Lemons and vinegar contain acids. Acids release CO₂ from limestone (CaCO₃), and this is how descalers work. Never taste anything in the lab.

once.soru: You dip litmus paper into lemon juice. What color does it turn?

secenekler.neden: Lemon contains acid, and litmus turns red in acid.
Litmus turns blue in base. Lemon is acidic.
Litmus is an indicator, and its color changes in acid.

cards.p: According to Arrhenius, an acid is a substance that releases H+ in water. The H+ bonds to water and forms H₃O+. A base is a substance that releases OH− in water. NH₃ is a base because it forms OH− with water.

etk.soru: Sort each substance by how it behaves in water: does it release H⁺ or form OH⁻?
ogeler: This is acetic acid, found in vinegar. It releases H⁺ in water (weak acid).
It has no OH in its structure, but it reacts with water and forms OH⁻.

cards.key: H₃O⁺ is the hydronium ion. The Arrhenius definition holds only for aqueous solutions.

once.soru: Which ion does HCl release when it dissolves in water?

secenekler.neden: HCl splits into H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in water. A substance that releases H⁺ in water is an acid.
HCl has no OH group. Substances that release OH⁻ are bases.
HCl splits almost completely into ions in water.

cards.p: According to Brønsted–Lowry, an acid is a proton (H+) donor and a base is a proton acceptor. An acid that gives away a proton leaves behind its conjugate base. For example, the conjugate base of CH₃COOH is CH₃COO−.

once.soru: What does water do in the reaction NH₃ + H₂O → NH₄⁺ + OH⁻?

secenekler.neden: Water gives an H⁺ to NH₃ and becomes OH⁻. Here it acts like an acid.
NH₃ is the one that accepts the proton and becomes NH₄⁺.
Water reacts, loses an H⁺ and becomes OH⁻.

once.soru: A little acid is added to pure water. What happens to [OH⁻]?

secenekler.neden: At 25 °C the product [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] is constant. So when H₃O⁺ goes up, OH⁻ goes down.
The acid adds H₃O⁺. The product stays constant, so OH⁻ cannot increase.
The product is constant. When one goes up, the other has to go down.

cards.h: pH, pOH and the pH scale
cards.p: pH is calculated as pH = −log[H₃O⁺]. For example, if [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻³ M, then pH = 3. At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14. pH 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic and above 7 is basic.

cards.h: Strong and weak acids and bases
cards.p: Strong acids and bases such as HCl, HNO₃, NaOH and KOH ionize completely in water. Weak ones such as CH₃COOH in vinegar and NH₃ ionize only slightly. Being strong does not mean being concentrated.

secenekler.neden: The acid with the larger Ka ionizes more. HF has the larger Ka.
This acid has the smaller Ka and ionizes less.
The Ka values differ. The one with the larger Ka is stronger.

cards.p: For a strong monoprotic acid, [H₃O⁺] equals the acid concentration. For example, 0.01 M HCl has a pH of 2. For weak acids, use [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C).
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='8' y='10' width='148' height='180' rx='6' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='var(--c2)'/><text x='82' y='30' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Strong acid</text><text x='82' y='56' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>0.01 M HCl</text><text x='82' y='78' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>[H₃O⁺] = 10⁻² M</text><text x='82' y='100' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>pH = 2</text><line x1='20' y1='116' x2='144' y2='116' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='82' y='136' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>0.01 M NaOH</text><text x='82' y='158' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>pOH = 2</text><text x='82' y='180' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>pH = 14 − 2 = 12</text><rect x='164' y='10' width='148' height='180' rx='6' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='var(--c5)'/><text x='238' y='30' font-size='13' fill='var(--c5)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Weak acid</text><text x='238' y='56' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>[H₃O⁺] ≈ √(K<tspan font-size='10' baseline-shift='sub'>a</tspan>·C)</text><text x='238' y='82' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>K<tspan font-size='10' baseline-shift='sub'>a</tspan> = 1×10⁻⁵</text><text x='238' y='105' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>C = 0.1 M</text><text x='238' y='127' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>√(10⁻⁶) = 10⁻³ M</text><text x='238' y='150' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>pH = 3</text><text x='238' y='172' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>ionized: 1%</text></svg>
cards.key: For strong bases, find pOH first. If you dilute a strong acid 10 times, the pH goes up by 1. 0.01 M HCl has a pH of 2, and 0.001 M HCl has a pH of 3.

once.soru: What is the pH of a 0.001 M HCl solution?

secenekler.neden: HCl ionizes completely. [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻³ M, so pH = 3.
That is the concentration. pH is the negative logarithm of the concentration.
11 is the pOH. The pH of an acid is below 7.

cards.p: When an acid reacts with a base, a salt and water form. The real event is H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ joining to make water, and heat is released. Stomach remedies called antacids work this way.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='asit-9' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='24' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O</text><text x='160' y='44' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>acid + base → salt + water</text><rect x='40' y='56' width='240' height='36' rx='6' fill='var(--acc)' fill-opacity='0.1' stroke='var(--acc)'/><text x='160' y='79' font-size='13' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>net: H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ → 2H₂O + heat</text><text x='160' y='116' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Antacid for heartburn:</text><text x='160' y='140' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O</text><text x='160' y='162' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂</text><text x='160' y='190' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Neutralization is exothermic.</text></svg>
cards.key: Antacids contain Mg(OH)₂ or NaHCO₃. Neutralization does not always give pH 7. The result depends on the salt that forms.

cards.p: H₂SO₄ can release two H⁺ and H₃PO₄ three. Ca(OH)₂ also releases two OH⁻. For complete neutralization, n(H⁺) = n(OH⁻).
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='24' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O</text><rect x='40' y='38' width='240' height='34' rx='6' fill='var(--acc)' fill-opacity='0.1' stroke='var(--acc)'/><text x='160' y='60' font-size='14' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>n(H⁺) = n(OH⁻)</text><text x='160' y='94' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>M<tspan font-size='9' baseline-shift='sub'>a</tspan> · V<tspan font-size='9' baseline-shift='sub'>a</tspan> · (number of H⁺) = M<tspan font-size='9' baseline-shift='sub'>b</tspan> · V<tspan font-size='9' baseline-shift='sub'>b</tspan> · (number of OH⁻)</text><text x='160' y='118' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>0.1 · 100 · 2 = 0.2 · V · 1  →  V = 100 mL</text><line x1='16' y1='132' x2='304' y2='132' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='16' y='152' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start'>HCl 1</text><text x='88' y='152' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start'>H₂SO₄ 2</text><text x='176' y='152' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start'>H₃PO₄ 3</text><text x='16' y='172' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start'>NaOH 1</text><text x='88' y='172' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start'>Ca(OH)₂ 2</text><text x='176' y='172' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start'>Al(OH)₃ 3</text><text x='160' y='194' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>CH₃COOH has 4 H but releases only 1 H⁺.</text></svg>
cards.key: For example, 100 mL of 0.1 M H₂SO₄ releases 0.02 mol of H⁺. 100 mL of 0.2 M NaOH neutralizes it. CH₃COOH releases only one H⁺.

once.soru: How many moles of NaOH are needed to fully neutralize 0.1 mol of H₂SO₄?

secenekler.neden: H₂SO₄ releases two H⁺. 0.2 mol of H⁺ needs 0.2 mol of OH⁻.
Each H₂SO₄ releases two H⁺, but each NaOH releases only one OH⁻.
The acid is diprotic. So you need more base, not less.

cards.p: The anion of a weak acid or the cation of a weak base reaches equilibrium with water, and this is called hydrolysis. So the pH of a salt depends on the strength of the acid and base that formed it.

+ H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻ (hydrolysis)</text></svg>
cards.key: The salt takes on the character of whichever side is strong. NH₄Cl is acidic and CH₃COONa is basic. If both are weak, compare Ka and Kb.

cards.p: Neutralizing an acid of unknown concentration drop by drop with a base of known concentration is called titration. When the acid is used up exactly, the equivalence point is reached and the pH jumps sharply.
cards.key: For a weak acid, the total amount of acid still counts. In a strong acid–strong base titration, the pH at the equivalence point is 7. In a weak acid–strong base titration, it is above 7.

once.soru: How many mL of NaOH of the same concentration are needed to neutralize 25 mL of HCl?

secenekler.neden: If the concentrations are equal, equal volumes contain equal moles. So 25 mL is enough.
That adds twice as much base. The acid runs out halfway, and the rest of the base is left over.
That is half of what is needed. Half of the acid stays un-neutralized.

cards.p: A solution that contains a weak acid and its conjugate base (CH₃COOH / CH₃COONa) is a buffer. When a little acid or base is added, its pH changes very little.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='asit-12' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--c2)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='22' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Adding 0.01 mol HCl to 1 L of solution</text><rect x='10' y='34' width='140' height='80' rx='6' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='var(--c2)'/><rect x='170' y='34' width='140' height='80' rx='6' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='var(--c3)'/><text x='80' y='54' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Pure water</text><text x='80' y='80' font-size='15' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>pH 7 → 2</text><text x='80' y='102' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>large change</text><text x='240' y='54' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Acetate buffer</text><text x='240' y='80' font-size='15' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>pH 4.74 → 4.66</text><text x='240' y='102' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>very small change</text><text x='160' y='136' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>0.1 M CH₃COOH + 0.1 M CH₃COONa</text><text x='160' y='160' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>added H₃O⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ → CH₃COOH + H₂O</text><text x='160' y='182' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>added OH⁻ + CH₃COOH → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O</text></svg>
cards.key: A weak base with its conjugate acid also makes a buffer. Blood is protected by the H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻ buffer. A buffer's capacity is limited.

cards.p: Active metals react with acids to form a salt and H₂. Cu, Ag and Au do not give H₂ with HCl. Amphoteric metals such as Al and Zn also release H₂ with strong bases.

cards.key: When diluting, always add acid to water, never water to acid. Cu and Ag react with HNO₃, but they release NO or NO₂, not H₂.

cards.p: Most nonmetal oxides are acidic (CO₂, SO₂). Oxides of active metals are basic (Na₂O, CaO). Al₂O₃ and ZnO are amphoteric, and CO, NO and N₂O are neutral oxides.

once.soru: What is the solution like when CO₂ dissolves in water?

secenekler.neden: CO₂ forms carbonic acid with water. That is where the slight sourness of soda comes from.
Basic solutions come from metal oxides. C is a nonmetal.
CO₂ reacts with water and forms an acid.

cards.p:
• An acid donates a proton and a base accepts one.
• At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14, and pH 7 is neutral.
• Strong acids and bases ionize completely, weak ones only partly.
• In neutralization, n(H⁺) = n(OH⁻). The salt that forms is not always neutral.
• Active metals form a salt and H₂ with acids.

quiz.q: What is the pH of a 0.005 M Ca(OH)₂ solution at 25 °C? (Ca(OH)₂ ionizes completely.)
quiz.e: Each Ca(OH)₂ releases two OH<sup>−</sup>. So [OH<sup>−</sup>] = 2 × 0.005 = 0.01 M and pOH = 2. The pH is 14 − 2 = 12.

quiz.q: At 25 °C, a 0.01 M solution of the weak acid HA has K<sub>a</sub> = 1×10⁻⁶. What is the pH of the solution?
quiz.e: [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(K<sub>a</sub>·C) = √(10⁻⁶ × 10⁻²) = √(10⁻⁸) = 10⁻⁴ M, so pH = 4. HCl at the same concentration would have a pH of 2.

quiz.q: Match each oxide to its type.
quiz.e: CO₂ forms an acid with water, and CaO forms a base. ZnO reacts with both acids and bases. CO reacts with neither, so it is neutral.

quiz.q: A 0.1 M CH₃COOH solution is titrated with 0.1 M NaOH. Which is true for the solution at the equivalence point at 25 °C?
quiz.e: At equivalence the solution contains CH₃COONa. The anion of the weak acid reacts with water and releases OH<sup>−</sup>, so the solution is basic.
y: Equal moles of a weak acid and a strong base do not give a neutral solution. CH₃COO<sup>−</sup> reacts with water and produces OH<sup>−</sup>.
At the equivalence point all of the acid has reacted. The CH₃COO<sup>−</sup> left in solution makes it basic.
The pH reaches 14 only with 1 M OH<sup>−</sup>. Here there is only acetate, a weak base.

redoks.title: Redox reactions
redoks.summary: Learn about electron transfer, oxidation states, balancing and the activity series.

cards.p: In some reactions one atom gives away electrons and another atom takes them. These are called redox reactions. When NaCl forms, Na gives away one electron and becomes Na+, and Cl takes that electron and becomes Cl−.

cards.key: Electrons don't disappear. An electron one atom gives away must be taken by another. "Redox" comes from the words reduction and oxidation.

once.soru: When sodium chloride forms, does the sodium atom take or give electrons?

secenekler.neden: Na is a metal, and it gives away 1 electron to become Na⁺. Cl takes this electron.
Cl is the one that takes an electron and becomes Cl⁻.
In NaCl electrons are transferred, not shared. This bond is called an ionic bond.

cards.p: The oxidation state is an atom's imagined charge in a compound. The atom that gives electrons is oxidized, and its oxidation state goes up. The atom that takes electrons is reduced, and its oxidation state goes down. The two always happen together.

cards.p: In a free element the oxidation state is 0, and in a monatomic ion it is the ion's charge. F is always −1, group 1A metals are +1 and group 2A metals are +2. In a neutral compound the oxidation states add up to 0.

cards.h: O and H: usually, not always
cards.p: In compounds O is usually −2, but in peroxides (H₂O₂) it is −1. H is usually +1, but in metal hydrides (NaH) it is −1. If the rules conflict, the F, 1A and 2A rules come first.

once.soru: If Na is +1 in NaH, what is the oxidation state of H?

secenekler.neden: The sum must be 0. +1 + x = 0, so x = −1. In metal hydrides H is −1.
H is usually +1, but here Na is already +1 and the sum wouldn't be 0.
H in a compound is not a free element.

cards.p: Call the unknown state x and write the sum rule. For NO₃<sup>−</sup>, x + 3(−2) = −1, so x = +5. For SO₃<sup>2−</sup>, x + 3(−2) = −2, so x = +4.

etk.soru: Find the oxidation state of each atom and match them.

cards.key: For C₂O₄²⁻, 2x + 4(−2) = −2, so x = +3. The same element can have different oxidation states. For example, N is −3 in NH₄⁺ and +5 in NO₃⁻.

once.soru: If O is −2 in CO₂, what is the oxidation state of C?

secenekler.neden: There are two O atoms, and together they contribute 2 · (−2) = −4.
The sum must be 0. The O atoms give −4, so C is +4.

cards.p: A substance that reduces something else is called a reducing agent. It gives electrons and is itself oxidized. An oxidizing agent takes electrons and is itself reduced. In Fe + 2Ag⁺, Fe is the reducing agent.

cards.key: Reactions in which a free element enters or leaves are usually redox. One exception is 3O₂ → 2O₃, because O stays at 0.

cards.p: If the same element is both oxidized and reduced, it is called disproportionation. In Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O, Cl goes from 0 both down to −1 and up to +1.

cards.key: Here Cl₂ is both the reducing agent and the oxidizing agent.

once.soru: In 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂, how does the oxidation state of O change? (O is −1 in H₂O₂)

secenekler.neden: O drops to −2 in H₂O and rises to 0 in O₂. So the same element is both reduced and oxidized.
O in O₂ has a state of 0. So there is also a rise from −1 to 0.
It goes from −1 to both −2 and 0.

cards.p: In acidic solution, split the reaction into half-reactions. Add H₂O for missing O, H+ for missing H and e− for the charge difference. Then make the electrons equal and add the half-reactions.

once.soru: In balancing, what is true about the numbers of electrons given and taken?

secenekler.neden: Electrons don't disappear. Every electron given is taken by another particle.
Otherwise extra electrons would be left somewhere, and that doesn't happen.
If the numbers aren't equal, charge and mass won't balance.

cards.p: In acidic solution, Mn in MnO₄<sup>−</sup> drops from +7 to +2. Write 4H₂O on the right and 8H<sup>+</sup> and 5e<sup>−</sup> on the left. The half-reaction Fe<sup>2+</sup> → Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>−</sup> is multiplied by five and added to it.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='12' y='22' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>Reduction (Mn: +7 → +2)</text><text x='12' y='44' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O</text><text x='12' y='72' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>Oxidation (Fe: +2 → +3), ×5</text><text x='12' y='94' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>5Fe²⁺ → 5Fe³⁺ + 5e⁻</text><line x1='8' y1='108' x2='312' y2='108' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.2'/><text x='12' y='128' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>Add: 5e⁻ cancels on both sides</text><rect x='8' y='138' width='304' height='56' rx='6' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='var(--c3)'/><text x='160' y='160' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ →</text><text x='160' y='184' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O</text></svg>
cards.key: Check the charges. The left side is −1 + 10 + 8 = +17 and the right side is +2 + 15 = +17, so the equation is balanced.

once.soru: If O is −2 in MnO₄⁻, what is the oxidation state of Mn?

secenekler.neden: The sum must equal the ion's charge, which is −1.
If it were +6, the sum would be −2.

cards.p: In basic solution, first balance as in acidic solution. Then add as many OH⁻ to both sides as there are H⁺. H⁺ and OH⁻ on the same side combine into H₂O. Cancel any water that appears on both sides.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='12' y='22' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>Basic solution: MnO₄⁻ → MnO₂ (Mn: +7 → +4)</text><text x='12' y='46' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>1) Balance as in acidic solution</text><text x='12' y='66' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>MnO₄⁻ + 4H⁺ + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 2H₂O</text><text x='12' y='92' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>2) Add 4OH⁻ to both sides; 4H⁺ + 4OH⁻ = 4H₂O</text><text x='12' y='112' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>MnO₄⁻ + 4H₂O + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 2H₂O + 4OH⁻</text><text x='12' y='138' font-size='11' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>3) Cancel the 2H₂O that appears on both sides</text><rect x='8' y='148' width='304' height='46' rx='6' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='var(--c3)'/><text x='160' y='176' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>MnO₄⁻ + 2H₂O + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 4OH⁻</text></svg>
cards.key: The final equation has no H⁺, but it has OH⁻. Don't forget to check the charge.

once.soru: Which one does not appear in an equation balanced in basic solution?

secenekler.neden: In basic solution H⁺ combines with OH⁻ and becomes water.
OH⁻ is the sign of basic solution, and it appears in the final equation.
Water is often used in balancing.

cards.p: The activity series of metals is K, Ca, Na, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Ni, Sn, Pb, (H), Cu, Hg, Ag, Pt, Au. A metal further left gives away electrons more easily.

etk.soru: Order from most active to least active in aqueous solution (hydrogen is included for comparison).

cards.key: A metal further left is a stronger reducing agent. Hydrogen is placed in the series for comparison. Cu, Ag and Au can stay unchanged in nature.

once.soru: Why does gold jewelry stay shiny for years?

secenekler.neden: Gold is very reluctant to give away electrons. So it doesn't oxidize in air.
Gold is actually a soft metal.
An active metal oxidizes quickly and tarnishes.

cards.p: A more active metal gives electrons to the ion of a less active metal and releases it as metal. For example, copper gets coated with silver in AgNO₃ solution (Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag).

cards.p: Metals more active than hydrogen (Zn, Fe) give H₂ with HCl. Semi-noble metals (Cu, Ag) don't release H₂. Noble metals (Au, Pt) dissolve only in aqua regia.

cards.key: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ is an example. Semi-noble metals give NO, NO₂ or SO₂ with HNO₃ and concentrated H₂SO₄. K, Na and Ca give H₂ even with cold water.

once.soru: You drop a piece of copper into HCl. Is H₂ gas released?

secenekler.neden: Cu is to the right of H in the activity series. So it can't reduce H⁺ ions.
The metals that release H₂ are those more active than hydrogen.
Copper releases no H₂ at all from HCl.

cards.p: In rusting, iron is oxidized. In burning, the fuel is oxidized and O₂ is reduced. Bleach whitens by oxidizing colored molecules. In photosynthesis CO₂ is reduced, and in respiration glucose is oxidized.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='10' y='8' width='146' height='88' rx='6' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='var(--c2)'/><text x='83' y='32' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Rusting</text><text x='83' y='58' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Fe → Fe³⁺ (rust)</text><text x='83' y='80' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>O₂ is reduced; moisture needed</text><rect x='164' y='8' width='146' height='88' rx='6' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='var(--c4)'/><text x='237' y='32' font-size='13' fill='var(--c4)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Burning</text><text x='237' y='58' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O</text><text x='237' y='80' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>C: −4 → +4</text><rect x='10' y='104' width='146' height='88' rx='6' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='var(--c1)'/><text x='83' y='128' font-size='13' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Bleach</text><text x='83' y='154' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>NaOCl: Cl has state +1</text><text x='83' y='176' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>reduced to Cl⁻ (−1)</text><rect x='164' y='104' width='146' height='88' rx='6' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='var(--c3)'/><text x='237' y='128' font-size='13' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>In living things</text><text x='237' y='154' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Photosynthesis: C +4 → 0</text><text x='237' y='176' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Respiration: C 0 → +4</text></svg>
cards.key: The oxidizing agent in bleach is NaOCl. Never mix bleach with muriatic acid, because toxic Cl₂ gas is released.

once.soru: When iron rusts, does it give or take electrons?

secenekler.neden: Fe goes from 0 to +3. So it is oxidized and gives electrons.
Oxygen is the one that takes electrons.
Rust is the oxidized form of iron.

cards.p:
• Oxidation is giving electrons, and the oxidation state goes up. Reduction is taking electrons, and the state goes down.
• Elements have a state of 0, and F is −1. O is usually −2 and H usually +1.
• The reducing agent is oxidized, and the oxidizing agent is reduced.
• In balancing, electrons given and taken are made equal.
• An active metal reduces the ion of a less active metal.

quiz.q: In acidic solution, the Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> ion is reduced to Cr<sup>3+</sup> ions. How many moles of electrons does 1 mol of Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> take?
quiz.e: In Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup>, 2x + 7(−2) = −2, so Cr is +6. Each Cr takes 3 e<sup>−</sup> as it drops from +6 to +3. For two Cr, a total of 6 mol of e<sup>−</sup> is needed.

quiz.q: Order these metals from most easily oxidized to least easily oxidized in aqueous solution.
quiz.e: The activity series is Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag. A metal further left gives away electrons more easily, so it is a stronger reducing agent.

quiz.q: Which of these are redox reactions? Sort them.
quiz.e: In rusting, Fe is oxidized. When methane burns, C is oxidized (−4 → +4) and O is reduced (0 → −2). H is +1 on both sides. Zn reduces Cu<sup>2+</sup>. In the reaction of Cl₂ with NaOH, Cl both drops to −1 and rises to +1. In neutralization and the precipitation of AgCl, no oxidation state changes.

quiz.q: Which is true for the reaction Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂?
o: Mg is reduced, HCl is the reducing agent
Mg is the reducing agent and is oxidized. H<sup>+</sup> is reduced
quiz.e: Mg goes from 0 to +2. So it gives electrons and is the reducing agent. H drops from +1 to 0. Cl stays −1 on both sides.
y: Mg gives electrons and is oxidized. A substance that gives electrons is the reducing agent. What is reduced is H<sup>+</sup>.
Cl is −1 on both sides of the reaction. The ones whose states change are Mg and H.
Mg goes from 0 to +2 and H from +1 to 0, so this is a redox reaction.

elektrokimya.title: Electrochemistry
elektrokimya.summary: Learn about cells, electrode potentials, the Nernst equation, electrolysis, Faraday's law and corrosion.

cards.p: If you connect two half-cells with a wire and a salt bridge, electrons flow through the wire. This setup is called a galvanic cell. The Zn electrode, which is oxidized, is the anode and the − terminal. The electrode where Cu2+ is reduced is the cathode and the + terminal.

etk.soru: Tap the parts of the Daniell cell.

noktalar.acik: Zn atoms give electrons and go into solution as Zn²⁺. This is oxidation.
Cu²⁺ ions take the electrons from the wire and build up as copper. This is reduction.
Electrons flow only through the wire. The voltmeter reads 1.10 V.
The salt bridge balances the charges by carrying ions. Anions go to the anode and cations to the cathode.
As the cell runs, the Zn²⁺ concentration rises.
As Cu²⁺ decreases, the blue color of the solution fades.

cards.key: If you drop Zn straight into CuSO₄, the energy comes out only as heat. As the cell runs, the Zn gets thinner and the Cu gets thicker.

cards.p: The salt bridge balances the charges. Anions go to the anode and cations to the cathode. Without the bridge the current stops. This cell is written as Zn | Zn2+ || Cu2+ | Cu.

once.soru: E° = −0.76 V for Zn²⁺/Zn and +0.34 V for Cu²⁺/Cu. Which ion is reduced more easily?

secenekler.neden: The ion with the larger E° takes electrons more easily.
A negative E° shows that the ion is hard to reduce.
The E° values are different.

cards.p: The standard cell voltage is E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. For the Daniell cell it is 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V. If E°cell is positive, the reaction is spontaneous, meaning it runs on its own.

once.soru: You add more Cu²⁺ to the cathode beaker of a Daniell cell. What happens to the cell voltage?

secenekler.neden: When the reactant ion increases, Q gets smaller and E gets larger.
The voltage falls when the product ion, Zn²⁺, increases.
The voltage depends on concentration.

cards.p: Current flows even when the two half-cells are the same but the concentrations differ. This is called a concentration cell. The dilute side is the anode, where Cu dissolves. The concentrated side is the cathode, where Cu2+ is reduced.

V</text></svg>
cards.key: For 0.01 M and 1 M solutions at 25 °C, E is about 0.059 V. When the concentrations become equal, the voltage drops to zero.

once.soru: One beaker holds 0.01 M Cu²⁺ and the other 1 M, each with a Cu rod. Does current flow?

secenekler.neden: The concentrations differ, so Q ≠ 1 and E is not zero. Current flows until the concentrations become equal.
E° is zero, but E depends on concentration.
Current flows at room temperature too.

cards.h: Why does a battery go dead?
cards.p: As the cell runs, Zn2+ builds up and Cu2+ decreases. So Q rises and E falls. In the end equilibrium is reached, with Q = K and E = 0. The cell is dead, but E° doesn't change.

cards.key: E° is a fixed value for standard conditions, and it doesn't change as the cell runs down.

once.soru: Are the electrodes of a dead battery used up?

secenekler.neden: A cell goes dead when the reaction reaches equilibrium. The electrodes may still be there.
What makes a cell dead is the voltage dropping to zero.
While the cell runs, the anode gets thinner and the cathode thicker.

cards.p: Driving a nonspontaneous redox reaction with an external source is called electrolysis. In an electrolytic cell the anode is the + terminal and the cathode is −. But oxidation still happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode.

once.soru: What happens to the reaction in the battery while you charge your phone?

secenekler.neden: The charger supplies energy from outside and drives the nonspontaneous direction. This is electrolysis.
The direction that runs on its own is the battery discharging.
During charging, the reaction runs in reverse.

cards.h: Electrolysis of molten NaCl and water
cards.p: When molten NaCl is electrolyzed, Na metal forms at the cathode and Cl₂ gas at the anode. Pure water conducts current poorly. Adding a little H₂SO₄ to water makes it conduct, and the water splits into H₂ and O₂.

once.soru: Aqueous NaCl solution is electrolyzed. What comes out at the cathode?

secenekler.neden: Water is reduced instead of Na⁺, and H₂ comes out at the cathode.
Na metal is obtained only from molten NaCl.
Cl₂ comes out at the anode.

cards.p: In plating, the object to be plated is the cathode and the plating metal is the anode. In refining, impure copper is the anode and pure copper the cathode. Ag and Au don't dissolve and settle as anode mud.

once.soru: You want to plate a spoon with silver. Which electrode do you make the spoon?

secenekler.neden: Ag⁺ is reduced at the cathode and builds up as metal. So the spoon must be the cathode.
Metal dissolves at the anode. If the spoon were the anode, it would get thinner.
Plating builds up only at the cathode.

cards.p: The charge passing through the circuit is Q = I·t. The charge of 1 mol of electrons is called 1 faraday, about 96 500 C. Cu2+ takes 2e−, so 0.1 mol of e− deposits 0.05 mol of Cu.

etk.soru: Current passes through CuSO₄ solution: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Change the current and the time. (1 F ≈ 96 500 C, Cu = 63.5 g/mol)

cards.key: If a 9.65 A current flows for 1000 s, it carries 9650 C, or 0.1 mol of e⁻. This charge deposits about 3.2 g of Cu. The same charge passes through cells connected in series.

cards.p: Rusting is a cell that runs on its own. Fe is oxidized, and O₂ is reduced together with water. Paint and galvanizing (zinc coating) protect iron. Mg connected to iron acts as a sacrificial anode.

once.soru: How many cells are in a car's 12 V battery?

secenekler.neden: Each lead-acid cell gives about 2 V. So 6 · 2 = 12 V.
One cell gives ≈2 V, not 1 V.
A single cell gives only ≈2 V.

cards.p:
• In a galvanic cell, a spontaneous redox reaction produces electricity, and the anode is −.
• E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, and coefficients don't change E°.
• As Q rises, E falls, reaching zero at equilibrium.
• Electrolysis drives a nonspontaneous reaction, and the anode is +.
• Charge is Q = I·t. 1 F ≈ 96 500 C.

quiz.q: Two cells are connected in series, one with AgNO₃ solution and the other with CuSO₄. When 5.4 g of Ag deposits at the cathode of the first cell, how many grams of Cu deposit at the cathode of the second? (Ag = 108, Cu = 63.5 g/mol)
quiz.e: 5.4 / 108 = 0.05 mol of Ag deposited, so 0.05 mol of e<sup>−</sup> passed. The same charge passes through cells in series. Since Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup> → Cu, 0.025 mol, or 0.025 × 63.5 ≈ 1.59 g of Cu deposits.

quiz.q: Sort each property under galvanic cell or electrolytic cell.
quiz.e: In a galvanic cell, a spontaneous redox reaction produces electricity and the anode is −. In electrolysis, an external source drives a nonspontaneous reaction, electrical energy turns into chemical energy and the anode is +.

quiz.q: For each electrolysis, match the product formed at that electrode.
quiz.e: In molten NaCl, Na<sup>+</sup> is reduced and Cl<sup>−</sup> is oxidized. In aqueous solution, Cu<sup>2+</sup> builds up as metal. Instead of Na<sup>+</sup>, water is reduced and gives H₂. Instead of SO₄<sup>2−</sup>, water is oxidized and gives O₂.

quiz.q: E° = −0.25 V for Ni<sup>2+</sup>/Ni and +0.80 V for Ag<sup>+</sup>/Ag. What is E° for a cell based on Ni + 2Ag<sup>+</sup> → Ni<sup>2+</sup> + 2Ag?
quiz.e: E° = 0.80 − (−0.25) = 1.05 V. Even though the Ag half-reaction is multiplied by 2, E° doesn't change. Using 2·0.80 is a common mistake.
y: E° is not multiplied by the coefficient. For Ag<sup>+</sup>, 0.80 V stays as it is, and the result is 0.80 − (−0.25).
E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. Instead of adding −0.25, you must subtract it. The right answer is 0.80 − (−0.25) = 1.05 V.
You swapped the cathode and the anode. Ag<sup>+</sup> is reduced, Ni is oxidized, and E° = +1.05 V.

organik-giris.title: Carbon and an introduction to organic chemistry
organik-giris.summary: Learn about carbon's bonds, its allotropes, the types of formulas and isomerism.

cards.p: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds. Carbon is mostly bonded to H, and also to O, N and S. CO, CO₂, carbonates and cyanides, however, count as inorganic.

etk.soru: All of these contain carbon. Which are organic compounds, and which are traditionally counted as inorganic?
ogeler: Urea, which Wöhler synthesized in 1828, is an organic compound.

cards.key: Carbides (such as CaC₂) are inorganic too. Pure carbon is not a compound at all.

once.soru: All of these contain carbon. Which one is an organic compound?

secenekler.neden: It is the simplest organic compound, with H bonded to C.
CO₂ is traditionally counted as inorganic.
Carbonates are inorganic.

cards.h: Wöhler and the end of vital force
cards.p: People once believed that organic matter could only form in living things, through a vital force. In 1828, Wöhler made urea from inorganic ammonium cyanate.

cards.key: This experiment shook the idea of vital force (vitalism). Later syntheses led to the idea being dropped completely.

once.soru: Can an organic substance be made in the lab, without a living thing?

secenekler.neden: Wöhler made urea from an inorganic substance. So a living thing is not required.
That was the old vital force idea, and experiments disproved it.
It can be synthesized in the lab without taking any substance from a living thing.

cards.p: Organic compounds are usually covalent. They have low melting points, most dissolve poorly in water, and they burn. Most inorganic compounds are ionic. They have high melting points, and their solutions conduct electricity.

once.soru: You heat a candle and some table salt. Which one melts sooner?

secenekler.neden: Wax is organic, and the attraction between its molecules is weak. So it melts at a low temperature.
Salt is an ionic solid and melts at 801 °C.
Their melting points are very different.

cards.p: Carbon has four valence electrons and forms four covalent bonds. With its own atoms, it builds long straight or branched chains and rings. It can form single, double and triple bonds.

cards.key: In stable organic compounds, C forms four bonds. C=C counts as two bonds and C≡C as three. Millions of organic compounds come from this property.

cards.p: Forms of the same element with different structures are called allotropes. In diamond, each C is bonded to four C atoms, and it is very hard. In graphite, each C is bonded to three C atoms, the layers slide, and it conducts electricity.

cards.key: Diamond does not conduct electricity. Allotropes are different forms of the same element. That is why both give CO₂ when they burn in enough O₂.

once.soru: Why does a pencil tip (graphite) leave a mark on paper so easily?

secenekler.neden: Graphite layers are held together by weak attraction. When rubbed on paper, the layers come apart and stay on the paper.
Diamond is the hard one. Graphite is soft.
Graphite does not melt while you write.

cards.p: Fullerene (C₆₀) is a molecule shaped like a soccer ball. Graphene is a single layer of graphite, one atom thick. A nanotube is graphene rolled into a cylinder, and it is both light and strong.

once.soru: Which element are fullerene, graphene and nanotubes made of?

secenekler.neden: They are all allotropes of carbon.
Silicon is a different element. These structures contain only C.
There is no metal in these structures.

cards.p: When carbon bonds, its orbitals mix and form hybrid orbitals. A C with four single bonds is sp³ (109.5°), a C with a double bond is sp² (120°), and a C with a triple bond is sp (180°) hybridized.

cards.p: End-to-end overlap of orbitals forms a sigma (σ) bond, and side-by-side overlap forms a pi (π) bond. A single bond is 1σ, a double bond is 1σ + 1π, and a triple bond is 1σ + 2π.

cards.p: According to VSEPR theory, the electron pairs on the central atom repel each other and spread as far apart as possible. Lone pairs repel more strongly. That is why the angle is 109.5° in CH₄, 107° in NH₃ and 104.5° in H₂O.

once.soru: Why is a water molecule bent rather than straight?

secenekler.neden: The two lone pairs on O push the H atoms and narrow the angle to 104.5°.
The two H atoms do not repel each other, but they do not attract either. Electron pairs decide the shape of the molecule.

secenekler.yazi: The O atom is very small
secenekler.neden: Electron pairs decide the shape, not atom size.

cards.p: A bond between atoms with different electronegativities is polar. If the bond dipoles do not cancel, the molecule is polar. H₂O and NH₃ are polar. Symmetric CH₄ and CO₂ are nonpolar.

once.soru: The C=O bonds in CO₂ are polar. Is the molecule polar?

secenekler.neden: In a linear molecule, the two dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.
Polar bonds are not enough. You also have to look at the molecule's geometry.
Polarity depends on the molecule's shape, not its state.

cards.h: Finding a formula by combustion analysis
cards.p: In combustion analysis, all the C ends up in CO₂ and all the H ends up in H₂O. From the products, you find the mass of C and H. If this total is less than the mass of the sample, the difference is oxygen. The ratio of the atoms gives the empirical formula.

once.soru: A substance burns and gives only CO₂ and H₂O. Which elements are certainly in the substance?

secenekler.neden: The O in the products can also come from O₂ in the air. Only C and H are certain.
Whether O is present is found by a mass calculation, not by looking at the products.
Since H₂O forms, H is present too.

cards.p: Compounds that contain only C and H are hydrocarbons. If the molecule has a functional group such as –OH or –COOH, that group largely decides its reactions.

once.soru: Is ethanol (C₂H₅OH) a hydrocarbon?

secenekler.neden: It contains an O atom. Hydrocarbons contain only C and H.
Ethanol has an –OH group.
Being a hydrocarbon depends on the elements, not the state.

cards.p: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures are called isomers. There are chain, position and functional group (for example, −OH) isomers. Ethanol and dimethyl ether are functional group isomers of each other.

cards.p:
• Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds. CO, CO₂ and carbonates are left out.
• Wöhler's synthesis of urea shook the idea of vital force.
• The angle is 109.5° for sp³, 120° for sp² and 180° for sp. A lone pair narrows the angle.
• A single bond is 1σ, a double bond 1σ+1π and a triple bond 1σ+2π.
• Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures.

quiz.q: Match the carbon atom in each molecule with its hybridization and bond angle.
quiz.e: In CO₂, C forms two double bonds, so it is sp hybridized and the angle is 180°. In HCHO, C has one double bond and is sp² hybridized (120°). In CH₃OH, C forms only single bonds and is sp³ hybridized (109.5°).

quiz.q: Sort each substance as organic or inorganic.
quiz.e: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, and the urea Wöhler synthesized is organic too. CO₂, carbonates (CaCO₃), cyanides (KCN) and carbides (CaC₂) contain carbon but count as inorganic.

quiz.q: How many sigma (σ) bonds are in the molecule CH₂=CH–C≡CH?
quiz.e: Each of the four C–H bonds and three C–C bonds contains one σ bond, so there are 4 + 3 = 7σ in total. The double bond adds another 1π, and the triple bond adds 2π.

quiz.q: Burning 4.6 g of a compound containing C, H and O completely gives 8.8 g of CO₂ and 5.4 g of H₂O. What is the empirical formula of the compound? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16 g/mol)
quiz.e: 8.8 g of CO₂ contains 0.2 mol of C (2.4 g). 5.4 g of H₂O is 0.3 mol and contains 0.6 mol of H (0.6 g). Oxygen is 4.6 − 3.0 = 1.6 g, or 0.1 mol. The ratio is 2 : 6 : 1, so the empirical formula is C₂H₆O. If you forget the two H atoms in H₂O, you get C₂H₃O.
y: 2.4 g of C and 0.6 g of H add up to 3.0 g. You left out the remaining 1.6 g of oxygen.
You didn't count the two H atoms in H₂O. 0.3 mol of water gives 0.6 mol of H, so the C:H ratio is 2:6.
You get 0.2 mol of C, 0.6 mol of H and 0.1 mol of O. The smallest ratio is 2:6:1, which doesn't fit CH₂O.

hidrokarbonlar.title: Hydrocarbons
hidrokarbonlar.summary: Learn the structure, naming and reactions of alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and benzene.

cards.p: Compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen are called hydrocarbons. Aliphatic hydrocarbons have no benzene ring. They are the single-bonded alkanes, the double-bonded alkenes and the triple-bonded alkynes. Aromatic hydrocarbons contain a benzene ring.

cards.key: Alkanes are nonpolar, do not dissolve in water and are lighter than water. Straight alkanes with C₁₈ or more are solids. Paraffin wax is a mixture of them.

cards.p: Alkanes are not very reactive. With enough oxygen, they burn and give CO2 and H2O. With too little oxygen, toxic CO forms. In light, a halogen atom replaces an H atom.

If it continues: CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄</text></svg>
cards.key: Because alkanes are saturated, they undergo substitution, not addition.

cards.p: If the two ends of a chain join, a cycloalkane forms. The general formula of cycloalkanes is CnH2n, and they are saturated. Cyclopropane has narrow angles, so it is strained and reactive. Cyclohexane is stable.

cards.key: Bromine water tells cyclohexane apart from an alkene. Under suitable conditions, though, cyclopropane can add Br₂.

once.soru: If the two ends of hexane (C₆H₁₄) join to form a ring, what is the formula?

secenekler.neden: As the ends join, each end loses one H. So the ring has two fewer H atoms.
When the end carbons bond to each other, each must give up one H.
The ring removes only two H atoms, and the single bonds stay.

cards.p: Alkenes contain a C=C double bond and are unsaturated. Their general formula is CnH2n. Their names use -ene instead of -ane, as in ethene and propene. Numbering starts from the end nearest the double bond.

once.soru: Ethene's formula is C₂H₄, and ethane's is C₂H₆. What is different in ethene?

secenekler.neden: When two carbons are joined by a double bond, there is no room left for two H atoms.
Two carbons cannot form a ring.
Both contain only C and H.

cards.p: In 2-butene, if the two CH3 groups are on the same side of the double bond, it is the cis isomer. If they are on opposite sides, it is the trans isomer. They are different substances with different boiling points.

once.soru: A double bond cannot rotate. In 2-butene, the two CH₃ groups can sit on the same side or on opposite sides. Are these the same substance?

secenekler.neden: The bond that cannot rotate keeps the two arrangements apart. So two isomers with different properties form.
Around a single bond, rotation would change the arrangement. Around a double bond, there is no rotation.
The difference lies in the molecule's structure, not in its state.

cards.p: One of the bonds in the double bond opens, and one atom is added to each of the two carbons. This is called addition. Adding H2 gives an alkane. Adding Br2 makes bromine water lose its color.

cards.key: When HX adds, the H bonds to the carbon that already has more hydrogens (Markovnikov's rule). For example, propene and HBr give 2-bromopropane.

cards.h: Polymerization: from ethene to plastic bags
cards.p: The double bonds of thousands of ethene molecules open, and the molecules join end to end to form polyethylene. The small unit is called a monomer, and the giant molecule a polymer. No double bonds remain in the polymer.

once.soru: Polyethylene, the plastic in shopping bags, is made from which small molecule?

secenekler.neden: Ethene's double bond opens, and the molecules join end to end.
Methane is saturated and has no double bond to open.
The benzene ring is stable, and it is not the unit of polyethylene.

cards.p: Alkynes contain a C≡C triple bond, and their general formula is CnH2n−2. The simplest alkyne is ethyne (acetylene), C2H2. When ethyne burns in oxygen, it gives a welding flame above 3000 °C.

cards.key: Addition to alkynes happens in two steps: the alkyne first becomes an alkene, then an alkane. 1 mol of alkyne uses 2 mol of H₂ or 2 mol of Br₂. 1 mol of alkene uses 1 mol.

cards.h: Naming alkynes and the terminal alkyne test
cards.p: Alkyne names end in -yne, as in ethyne, propyne and 1-butyne. If the triple bond is at the end of the chain, it is a terminal alkyne. Terminal alkynes give a precipitate with ammoniacal AgNO3.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='22' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Name: alkane root + -yne · ethyne, propyne, butyne</text><text x='12' y='58' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>1-butyne</text><text x='12' y='74' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>terminal alkyne</text><text x='170' y='64' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>H–C<tspan fill='var(--c2)'>≡</tspan>C–CH₂–CH₃</text><text x='306' y='64' font-size='11' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>precipitate</text><text x='12' y='110' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>2-butyne</text><text x='12' y='126' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>internal alkyne</text><text x='170' y='116' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>CH₃–C<tspan fill='var(--c2)'>≡</tspan>C–CH₃</text><text x='306' y='116' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>no precipitate</text><rect x='8' y='146' width='304' height='50' rx='6' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.1' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='1.2'/><text x='160' y='166' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Ammoniacal AgNO₃ → white precipitate</text><text x='160' y='185' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Ammoniacal CuCl → red-brown precipitate</text></svg>
cards.key: 2-butyne gives no precipitate. So this test tells a terminal alkyne apart from an internal one. CuCl also gives a precipitate.

once.soru: 1-butyne and 2-butyne have the same formula. Which one has ≡C–H at its end?

secenekler.neden: The triple bond is at carbon 1, and the end carbon carries an H.
The triple bond is in the middle, and both ends carry CH₃.
In 2-butyne, the triple bond is not at the end.

cards.p: In benzene (C6H6), 6 π electrons spread around the ring (delocalized), and all the C–C bonds are equal. Because of this stability, benzene undergoes substitution instead of addition.

once.soru: The pump says "95 octane". What does the octane rating show?

secenekler.neden: High-octane gasoline does not ignite too early in the engine.
Gasolines have similar energy. The octane rating measures resistance to early ignition.
Sulfur is measured separately. The octane rating shows resistance to knocking.

cards.p:
• Alkanes contain single bonds, alkenes double bonds and alkynes triple bonds.
• A longer alkane chain raises the boiling point, and branching lowers it.
• Alkanes and benzene undergo substitution. Alkenes and alkynes undergo addition and decolorize bromine water.
• For cis-trans isomerism, both carbons of the double bond must carry different groups.

quiz.q: How many moles of O₂ are used when 1 mol of butane (C₄H₁₀) burns completely?
quiz.e: C₄H₁₀ + 6.5O₂ → 4CO₂ + 5H₂O. 4 CO₂ need 8 O, and 5 H₂O need 5 O. That is 13 O atoms in total, or 6.5 mol of O₂.

quiz.q: Sort each hydrocarbon as saturated or unsaturated.
quiz.e: Alkanes and cycloalkanes contain only single bonds and are saturated. Alkenes, ending in -ene, have C=C, and alkynes, ending in -yne, have C≡C. These are unsaturated.

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH(C₂H₅)–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃?
quiz.e: The longest chain has 6 C (hexane). Numbering from the end nearest the branches puts methyl on carbon 2 and ethyl on carbon 3. Branches are written in alphabetical order, so the name is 3-ethyl-2-methylhexane.
y: Branches are written in alphabetical order. So ethyl (e) comes before methyl (m).
Numbering starts from the end nearest a branch. The set 2,3 is lower than 4,5.
The parent chain has 6 C. You also need to include the CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ end on the right.

quiz.q: Which one shows cis-trans (geometric) isomerism?
quiz.e: In 2-butene, each double-bonded carbon carries two different groups (CH₃ and H). In the others, at least one double-bonded carbon carries two H atoms. So not every alkene shows cis-trans isomerism.
y: In ethene, each carbon carries two H atoms. A carbon with two identical groups does not show cis-trans isomerism.
In propene, the end carbon carries two H atoms. Geometric isomerism needs different groups on each carbon of the double bond.
In 1-butene, the double bond is at the end and C1 carries two H atoms. So it has no cis-trans isomers.

fonksiyonel-gruplar.title: Functional groups
fonksiyonel-gruplar.summary: Learn about alcohols, ethers, aldehydes, ketones, acids, esters, amines and amides.

cards.p: The group of atoms that decides a compound's reactions and properties is called a functional group. The carbon skeleton is the carrier, and the group gives the character. In formulas, R is the hydrocarbon part.

once.soru: Why does the name of ethanol (C₂H₅OH), the alcohol in cologne, end in -ol?

secenekler.neden: Alcohol names are made by adding -ol to the alkane name.
There is no O₂ gas in the molecule. The O atom is inside the −OH group.
The name comes from the group, not from the state of the substance.

cards.p: Alcohols form hydrogen bonds between their −OH groups. That is why they boil at much higher temperatures than similar alkanes. They also form hydrogen bonds with water, but solubility drops as the chain gets longer.

cards.p: Ethanol is made when yeast breaks down sugar without oxygen. This process is called fermentation. Methanol is very toxic, and even a small amount can cause blindness or death.

cards.key: In the body, methanol turns into formaldehyde and formic acid. It cannot be told apart from ethanol by smell or look. The poison in bootleg liquor is also methanol.

once.soru: When yeast is added to dough, the dough rises. What forms as the yeast breaks down sugar?

secenekler.neden: In fermentation, sugar turns into ethanol and CO₂. The CO₂ makes the dough rise.
Yeast does not make methanol. The product of fermentation is ethanol.
A gas makes the dough rise, and that gas is CO₂.

once.soru: In winter, what is added to the water in a car radiator to keep it from freezing?

secenekler.neden: Ethylene glycol lowers the freezing point of water and is the main ingredient of antifreeze.
Salt also delays freezing, but it makes metal rust.
Sugar is not used in radiators, because it settles out and clogs them.

cards.h: Aldehydes and ketones: the carbonyl group
cards.p: The C=O group is called a carbonyl. At the end of a chain (−CHO), it makes an aldehyde, and between two carbons, it makes a ketone. Their names end in -al (ethanal) and -one (propanone).

once.soru: The acetone in nail polish remover is a ketone. Where is the C=O in a ketone?

secenekler.neden: In a ketone, the carbonyl carbon has a carbon on each side.

secenekler.yazi: At the end of the chain
secenekler.neden: A C=O at the end (−CHO) is an aldehyde.
Acetone is a three-carbon molecule with no ring.

cards.p: Compounds with a carboxyl group (−COOH) are called carboxylic acids. Formic acid in ants and acetic acid in vinegar are examples. They are weak acids. With bases, they give a salt and water, and with active metals, they give H₂.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='80' y='30' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>HCOOH</text><text x='240' y='30' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>CH₃COOH</text><text x='80' y='48' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>formic acid (ants)</text><text x='240' y='48' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>acetic acid (vinegar)</text><text x='160' y='84' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺</text><text x='160' y='104' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>weak acid: equilibrium lies far to the left</text><rect x='20' y='120' width='280' height='20' rx='3' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c1)'/><rect x='296' y='120' width='4' height='20' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='20' y='160' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start'>≈ 99% CH₃COOH molecules</text><text x='300' y='160' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='end'>≈ 1% ions</text><text x='160' y='186' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>0.1 M acetic acid, 25 °C</text></svg>
cards.key: Their names end in -oic acid, as in ethanoic acid. They give CO₂ with carbonates. Because its structure resembles an aldehyde, HCOOH also gives a positive Tollens test.

once.soru: Vinegar fizzes when you add a little carbonate. Which group does the acid in vinegar carry?

secenekler.neden: The carboxyl group gives off H⁺. So the carbonate releases CO₂ foam.
An alcohol's −OH group is neutral and does not make carbonate fizz.
The aldehyde group is not an acid.

cards.p: When a carboxylic acid and an alcohol are heated with concentrated H₂SO₄, an ester and water form. The reaction is reversible, and the reverse is called ester hydrolysis. Small esters smell like fruit.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='20' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Esterification (concentrated H₂SO₄, heat)</text><text x='85' y='56' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>CH₃−CO<tspan fill='var(--c2)'>OH</tspan></text><text x='160' y='56' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>+</text><text x='235' y='56' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><tspan fill='var(--c2)'>H</tspan>O−C₂H₅</text><text x='85' y='74' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>acetic acid</text><text x='235' y='74' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>ethanol</text><text x='160' y='106' font-size='15' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>⇌</text><text x='176' y='105' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>reversible</text><text x='85' y='140' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>CH₃<tspan fill='var(--c1)'>−COO−</tspan>C₂H₅</text><text x='170' y='140' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>+</text><text x='235' y='140' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><tspan fill='var(--c2)'>H₂O</tspan></text><text x='85' y='158' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>ethyl acetate (ester)</text><text x='235' y='158' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>water</text><text x='160' y='186' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'>Water: the acid's −OH + the alcohol's H</text></svg>
cards.key: An ester's name gives the alcohol's alkyl group first, then the acid with the ending -oate, as in ethyl ethanoate. Isoamyl acetate smells like bananas, and ethyl butanoate like pineapple.

cards.p: Fats are esters formed from the three −OH groups of glycerol and three fatty acids. When a fat is heated with NaOH, glycerol and soap form. This process is called saponification.

cards.p: Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which carbon groups replace the H atoms, and they are weak bases. In an amide, N is bonded to a carbonyl carbon (−CONH−). The peptide bond in proteins is an amide bond.
